summary.text: 东 means “east” and is the simplified form of 東, adapted from its cursive writing. Its present shape is a single graph, not separate 日 and 木 components.

formation.text: Derived: 东 is a cursive-derived form of 東. For the older graph, a significant but disputed analysis sees a tied bag and proposes that its sign was reused for “east” because the object’s name may have sounded like the direction word. The object’s ancient name and pronunciation are not known, so this sound-based explanation remains a proposal. Shuowen preserves another historical interpretation, reading 東 through 木 and 日 within 木; that account does not establish the graph’s early origin.

components.text: 东 is one whole graph derived from cursive 東, not a combination of independent 日 and 木 parts. In a disputed analysis of the older graph, 東 depicts a tied bag; this reading is not settled.

history.text: 东 is adapted from cursive writing of 東. The curated oracle-style and Shang bronze-style images are modern redraws of early-form traditions; the seal-style image represents the later Shuowen tradition. They show different forms, but do not establish a step-by-step sequence.

Shuowen preserves the historical explanation that 東 is formed from 木 and was also understood as 日 within 木. This influential reading is not confirmation of the early graph’s origin; a competing discussion considers possible 日 and 木 interpretations without establishing them as the origin.

uncertainties.text: The tied-bag interpretation is a significant but disputed account of early 東. Many early occurrences are reported in names and ritual contexts rather than clear uses meaning “bag,” so the graph’s original referent remains unsettled.

The proposed reuse of a bag sign for “east” depends on a sound resemblance between the object’s name and the direction word. The object’s ancient name and pronunciation are not recovered; reconstructions of 東 alone cannot establish them.

An oracle-bone use of 東 for the eastern region is reported, though the cited inscription was not independently inspected as an artifact. The received poem also uses 東 directionally, but its composition date and earliest physical witness are unresolved.

senses.period: Early inscriptional contexts reported; exact first attestation unresolved
senses.text: 東 is reported in an oracle-bone inscription for the eastern region, as well as in later early inscriptions referring to eastern territory. The received poem 小星 also uses it directionally, but its exact composition date and earliest physical witness are unresolved.

東 is also recorded with the meaning “host” or “landlord.” A traditional explanation links this sense to the host’s position on the east side, and a Tang literary example is reported. The first attestation and the path from “east” to this sense are unresolved.
The common modern meaning is the east or something situated toward the east.

limitations.text: The proposed bag-name origin is an account of reusing a written sign for a similar-sounding word, not a demonstrated semantic change; the source word’s name and sound remain unknown here.

The host or landlord explanation and its reported literary example do not establish a dated development from “east.” Spring and toilet senses also appear in dictionary records, but their chronology and semantic links are unresolved.

items.period: Shang dynasty oracle-bone script tradition; exact specimen dating not supplied on Commons page
items.tradition: Oracle-bone script style; modern vector redraw
items.caption: This oracle-script style redraw of 東 has a tall enclosing outline with several interior openings. A database interprets early forms as a tied bag, though that proposed original sense remains disputed.
items.alt: Black oracle-script style character with a tall, rounded enclosure and several white openings.
items.selection_reason: A useful early graphic example for the proposed bag interpretation; its visible structure can be described without treating the drawn openings as proof of what the graph depicted.
items.rights: Public domain dedication stated on the Commons file page for this SVG representation.

items.period: Late Shang dynasty, as attributed in the Commons source note to 東父乙尊
items.tradition: Shang bronze inscription style; modern vector redraw
items.caption: This Shang bronze-script style redraw of 東 has a rounded outer contour crossed by horizontal and vertical strokes, creating a grid-like interior. The file page associates it with the late-Shang 東父乙尊; the sack interpretation of early forms is disputed.
items.alt: Black rounded bronze-script style form with crossing interior strokes and multiple openings.
items.selection_reason: Its distinct, grid-like interior provides a useful early-form comparison alongside the oracle-style candidate. It is a modern redraw associated by its file page with a named bronze source, not an artifact photograph.

items.period: Shuowen seal-script tradition (Eastern Han dictionary tradition); redraw uploaded in 2015
items.tradition: Seal script; modern Inkscape vector redraw
items.caption: This seal-script style redraw of 東 has a rounded central enclosure divided by horizontal and vertical strokes, with strokes extending above and below. Shuowen records an interpretation involving 日 within 木; that historical explanation does not establish the graph's earliest origin.
items.alt: Black seal-script style form with a divided rounded center and strokes extending above and below.
items.selection_reason: The form makes a useful comparison for the historically influential Shuowen explanation, while the visible shape and that account do not settle the graph’s early origin.

limitations.text: These are modern vector redraws rather than photographs of ancient inscriptions. Early forms are interpreted as a tied bag in some analyses, but this account is disputed, and the surviving evidence does not establish the depicted object's spoken name or prove the proposed sound-loan pathway to “east.”
Shuowen preserves a historical 日-within-木 interpretation; it is not confirmation that the graph originated as a sun-and-tree compound.
